Median regression without the gross-error rule gave *g* = -0.059, \[-0.075, -0.041\]. Replacing the curvature term by separate slopes for near and far anchors showed that the slope for anchors more than one log unit from the true value differed from the slope near the true value by -0.21, \[-0.28, -0.13\]; the slope was 0.31, \[0.25, 0.36\], near the true value and 0.10, \[0.04, 0.17\], further away, so far anchors still pulled estimates, but less (both reported post hoc). Without Bahník (2021) the estimate was similar but very imprecise, *g* = -0.045, \[-0.36, 0.27\]. The across-cell slope stayed positive and imprecise in most checks: with design covariates, *d* = 0.044, \[-0.021, 0.108\]; with the largest anchor distance as the extremity measure, 0.035, \[-0.009, 0.079\]; with the log ratio of the anchors, 0.017, \[-0.014, 0.049\]. Without Weber et al. (2021), a study from the OpAQ team whose item coding may be affected by item mix-ups that an unpublished 2026 corrigendum reported for a related publication, the slope was 0.065, \[0.006, 0.124\], the only check in which the interval excluded zero. The raw-scale anchoring index, which the preregistration designated as descriptive because a constant log-scale weight does not imply a constant raw-scale index, gave -0.008, \[-0.077, 0.062\]. ## Exploratory analyses The following analyses were not preregistered. *Both sides of the true value.* The curvature was negative both for anchors below the true value, *g* = -0.037, \[-0.048, -0.027\], and for anchors above it, *g* = -0.054, \[-0.091, -0.017\]. *Item by item.* In each of the 15 cells with at least 20 estimates both within and beyond one log unit of the true value, the slope for far anchors was lower than the slope for near anchors (median difference -0.23). *Standardised effect sizes.* Across cells, Hedges’ *g* rose with extremity by 0.40 per log unit, \[0.24, 0.55\] (Figure 3, panel B), in line with Röseler & Schütz (2022). The same cells therefore show a rising standardised effect and no detectable change in proportional pull. *Extremity relative to response spread.* The across-cell extremity measure ignores how uncertain people are about each quantity. When we divided extremity by the spread of log estimates within each anchor condition (a measure that is itself affected by anchoring), the slope turned negative, *d* = -0.023, \[-0.037, -0.010\]. When we instead entered extremity and spread as separate predictors, the extremity slope was 0.028, \[-0.050, 0.106\]. The two specifications disagree, and a ratio predictor can produce spurious associations when its denominator is related to the outcome’s precision, so this analysis does not settle whether the across-cell pattern reflects how anchors were placed relative to people’s uncertainty. *Relaxed calibration.* To check whether the model failures stem from the calibration to Jacowitz and Kahneman’s index, we drew 300 parameter sets per model from wide ranges without calibration and simulated each on the OpAQ designs. None of these draws reproduced the observed *b*, *g*, *d* and mean index jointly (all four inside their observed 95% confidence intervals); with 300 draws per model, this shows that such parameter settings are rare, not that none exist. Within-item *b* and *g* together were reproduced by 24 of 300 M4 draws, 9 M1R draws and 7 M3 draws, and by no M1 or M2 draw; the across-cell *d* and mean index together were reproduced by 37 M2 draws and 11 M1 draws, and by no M3 or M4 draw. *Constant weight on the raw scale.* M2 assumes a constant weight on the log scale. We also simulated a constant weight on the raw scale (the estimate is a weighted average of anchor and belief in raw units; weights drawn from .30 to .60; 300 replicates). Passed through the H1 estimator, this model predicted a negative pooled curvature, *g* = -0.059, \[-0.084, -0.034\], an interval that contains the observed value, because on the log scale raw averaging flattens the response to anchors below the belief. It predicted opposite curvatures on the two sides of the true value, however: negative below (-0.054, \[-0.077, -0.032\]) and positive above (0.134, \[0.101, 0.165\]). The observed curvature above the true value was negative (-0.054), which contradicts raw-scale constant weighting. The preregistered pooled test alone would not have ruled out this model. *Study-specific estimates.* The curvature was negative in Bahník (2021), *g* = -0.035, \[-0.046, -0.024\], and in the Cologne cathedral item of Imhoff & Barker (2023), -0.089, \[-0.148, -0.031\]; it was imprecise in Frech et al. (2021), -0.083, \[-0.32, 0.15\], and positive in the two items of Yoon et al. (2021), whose anchors were participants’ own height or age, 0.093, \[0.021, 0.166\]. Imhoff & Barker (2023) reported a linear relation between anchor and estimate for the Cologne cathedral item on the raw scale; a linear raw-scale relation also produces a declining log-scale elasticity for anchors below the belief, so this item alone does not discriminate between log-scale plausibility models and raw-scale averaging. ## Sensitivity analyses These analyses were added after a code review and were not preregistered. *Calibration scale.* The preregistered calibration compared the models’ log-scale anchoring index with Jacowitz and Kahneman’s value of about .49, which they computed on the raw scale. Recalibrating every model to a raw-scale index accepted largely the same parameter values (M1: 22 of 24; M1R: 52 of 56; M2: 28 of 30; M3: 10 of 11; M4: 244 of 250 of the originally accepted grid points were also accepted), and new predictions from the recalibrated models led to the same conclusion: only M1R survived the shape criteria. *Dependence on single studies (H1).* Leaving out any one of the three smaller studies left the curvature negative with confidence intervals excluding zero (*g* from -0.043 to -0.038). Adding study-level random effects gave *g* = -0.041, \[-0.058, -0.024\]. The single fixed-anchor item with 20 anchor levels (the supplementary task of Imhoff & Barker, 2023, Study 2) showed a negative curvature on its own, *g* = -0.089, \[-0.148, -0.031\]. *Influence and clustering (H2).* The across-cell slope was not robust. With study-clustered robust standard errors, *d* = 0.050, \[-0.048, 0.148\]. The ten most precise cells carried 61% of the inverse-variance weight; without them, *d* = 0.033, \[-0.032, 0.099\]. Leaving out one study at a time gave slopes between 0.026 and 0.070. Resampling participants within studies gave a median slope of 0.044 (this interval, \[0.022, 0.069\], reflects participant sampling only, not variation between items), and converting the Chicago responses from millions and retaining that cell gave *d* = 0.047, \[-0.017, 0.111\]. # Discussion Within items, anchors lost proportional pull as they moved away from the true value. Near the truth, the local elasticity was 0.31; for anchors a factor of 2.7 from the truth it was 0.23, and for anchors a factor of 7.4 away, 0.14. The decline appeared on both sides of the true value, in every item with enough near and far anchors, and in the one fixed-anchor item with many anchor levels. Across two-anchor studies, where authors chose one anchor pair per item, the anchoring index showed no detectable decline, and its point estimate leaned the other way. ## What the within-item result rules out The negative curvature contradicts two simple implementations. Anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps predicts that far anchors keep more of their distance, because a bounded number of bounded steps cannot correct a large gap; the data show the reverse. Constant-weight integration on the log scale predicts no change in proportional pull; it too is contradicted. Constant weighting on the raw scale predicts the observed pooled curvature, but also a rising elasticity above the true value, which the exploratory side-specific estimates contradict. The implementations that predict a decline on both sides share one feature: the anchor’s influence is limited by how plausible it is. This holds for adjustment that stops at the edge of the plausible range (Epley & Gilovich, 2006; Mussweiler & Strack, 2001) and for integration that discounts implausible anchors (Turner & Schley, 2016; Wegener et al., 2001). The resource-rational variant can also produce a decline, but its calibrated versions did not reproduce the observed combination of elasticity and curvature. The result fits earlier experiments with few anchor levels in which implausible anchors had proportionally smaller effects (Chapman & Johnson, 1994; Mussweiler & Strack, 2001; Wegener et al., 2001), the distance-decaying anchoring weight of Barrera-Lemarchand et al. (2024), and the levelling-off of assimilation to symbolic anchors in dot estimation (Imhoff & Barker, 2023). It extends these findings to general-knowledge magnitudes, to anchors far outside the plausible range, and to a proportional outcome. In a dot-estimation task with anchors 35% or 70% away from the true value, the more distant anchors produced larger estimation errors (Mayer & Rebholz, 2024); a larger absolute effect is compatible with a declining proportional pull, so the two findings do not conflict. Relative to the overall strength of anchoring, the decline was smaller than the calibrated versions of M3 and M4 predicted: their intervals for ρ lay below the observed value, and far anchors still had a positive slope. Far anchors thus pulled estimates more than a hard plausibility boundary or a steep plausibility discount allows, at least within the calibrated parameter ranges. A mixture in which the weight of an anchor falls gradually but does not vanish could describe this. The data do not identify such a model, and we did not test one. ## The across-cell pattern The across-cell analysis did not reproduce the within-item decline, and no model with a single parameter set reproduced both patterns. Two explanations are plausible, and our data cannot fully separate them. First, extremity measured against the true value is not extremity measured against people’s uncertainty. Researchers may place anchors further from the truth for quantities that people know poorly. An anchor ten times the true population of a city may be less implausible than an anchor twice the height of a familiar building. When we scaled extremity by the spread of estimates, the across-cell slope turned negative, as the within-item analysis and the plausibility accounts predict, but entering spread as a separate predictor left the extremity slope positive and imprecise. Because the spread is itself affected by anchoring, neither analysis resolves the question. Second, the two sets differ in anchor type: the within-item set is mostly random anchors, and the across-cell set only fixed or relevant anchors. The models make the same shape predictions for both, but it is possible that informative anchors lose less pull with extremity than anchors people know to be random. The fixed-anchor stratum of the within-item set pointed in the same direction as the random-anchor stratum but was too small for the preregistered test, and only one fixed-anchor item had enough anchor levels to show the decline on its own. The divergence also bears on how moderator analyses of anchoring should be read. In the same cells, the standardised effect rose with extremity while the proportional index did not change detectably. Meta-analytic findings that larger anchor distances produce larger standardised effects (Röseler & Schütz, 2022) therefore say little about whether extreme anchors are more influential per unit of distance. Tests of anchoring theories need a proportional outcome and variation in extremity that the researcher controls. ## Limitations The primary evidence rests largely on one study. Thirteen of the 20 within-item cells, and 83% of the within-item estimates, come from Bahník (2021), in which participants compared 13 random anchors with 13 different lengths and heights. Without this study the within-item curvature had the same sign but a confidence interval too wide to be informative. The random anchors also differ from the fixed anchors that dominate applied settings. The preregistered test of the fixed-anchor stratum was not informative; in an exploratory analysis, the one fixed-anchor item with 20 anchor levels showed the same decline, but it is a single item. A direct test of the extremity function for informative anchors needs experiments that present many anchor levels for many items. Second, extremity was measured relative to the true value, not relative to each participant’s belief. Where people systematically over- or underestimate a quantity, the anchor’s distance from their belief differs from its distance from the truth. The simulations included item-level bias to account for this, and the curvature was negative on both sides of the true value. However, a study that elicits unanchored estimates or plausible ranges from the same participants would give a cleaner measure. Third, the models were specified on the log scale and calibrated to a single external benchmark. The shape predictions of M1, M2, M3 and M4 follow from their structure and held across all calibrated parameter values, but the level predictions depend on the calibration, and the resource-rational model’s predictions depend strongly on its time cost and on how uncertain people are. That this model survived our tests reflects the width of its predictions more than a close fit. Formal tests of resource-rational anchoring need independent measures of the time cost and of people’s uncertainty. Fourth, OpAQ harmonises data from many studies, and its codes do not always match the original designs: the two items of Yoon et al. (2021) used participants’ own height or age as anchors, and the anchors of the Cologne cathedral item were described by its authors as random. Harmonisation can also introduce errors. We found one item whose responses were recorded in different units from its anchors and true value, and an unpublished 2026 corrigendum, posted on the OpAQ project page for a related publication by the same group, suggests that the item coding of another study (Weber et al., 2021) may contain errors. Our rules removed the first; excluding the second made the across-cell slope positive and significant. We used only positive ratio-scale quantities with open response scales, so the results do not speak to dates, percentages, bounded scales or preferences. ## Conclusion Within the same questions, extreme anchors pulled estimates by a smaller share of their distance than moderate anchors. The evidence comes mostly from random anchors for lengths and heights in one study, with the same pattern in the one fixed-anchor item that had many anchor levels. It contradicts anchor-and-adjust with a fixed number of steps and constant-weight integration, and supports accounts in which an anchor’s influence is limited by its plausibility, although the decline was weaker than simple plausibility models predict. Across studies with researcher-chosen anchors, the pattern was not visible. Whether deliberately chosen, informative anchors, such as opening offers in negotiations, also show diminishing returns to extremity cannot be answered with these data. The extremity function should be estimated within items, with proportional measures and with anchors of the kind used in practice. # Acknowledgements The text of this article, including the abstract, tables and figure captions, was generated by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic) on 27-28 September 2026, as described under Use of AI tools in the Method section. The revision substantially addresses the round-1 major requests. A2, A4, A5, X2, X3, X4 and X6 are adequately resolved; A1 is largely resolved by narrowing the scope. A3, X1 and X5 are now reported more fairly, but the interpretation still needs work.

1. **MAJOR — Measures, Abstract and Conclusion.** The manuscript defines “proportional pull” as a *local elasticity*, then concludes that extreme anchors pull estimates by a smaller *share of the distance between belief and anchor*. Those are different quantities. The model uses distance from the true value, while participants’ unanchored beliefs were not measured. **Fix:** State the primary finding as a decline in local response to changes in the anchor. Use “share of the belief–anchor gap” only if that share can be estimated against a justified belief baseline.

2. **MAJOR — Model adequacy and Discussion.** The conclusion says the result “supports” plausibility-based accounts, although the calibrated M3 and M4 predictions miss both relative curvature and the across-cell slope. M1R misses curvature and the post-hoc joint check of elasticity and curvature. Negative curvature is consistent with a plausibility mechanism, but these tests do not establish one. **Fix:** State prominently that no calibrated model adequately explains the combined results; describe plausibility as one possible account of the within-item shape. This completes the interpretive response to A3, X1 and X5.

3. **MINOR — H3 decision rules and Table 3.** The prose says a model is contradicted when curvature “(*g* or ρ)” falls outside its interval, yet M1R is retained despite *g* falling outside. **Fix:** Write the exact logical rule—whether rejection requires both curvature measures to miss—and explain why either measure can qualify a model for retention.

4. **MINOR — H2 standard errors.** The formula `1.2533 × MAD / √n` is appropriate if MAD has been scaled to estimate the standard deviation under a normal model. If it means the unscaled median absolute deviation, it understates the standard error. **Fix:** Specify the MAD convention used in code and confirm that the stated formula matches it.

5. **MINOR — Results, “Item by item.”** The claim that all 15 eligible cells had lower far-anchor slopes sits uneasily beside the positive quadratic curvature reported for Yoon et al. These fits can differ, but the reader cannot see why here. **Fix:** Identify the 15 cells and briefly reconcile the two summaries, or narrow the “every item” claim.

6. **MINOR — Table 2 and Data availability.** Table 2 calls *b* “average elasticity,” although *b* is the fitted elasticity at the true value. The repository link is still a placeholder, preventing verification of the preregistration and frozen predictions. **Fix:** Correct the column heading and add the repository link before submission.

**Recommendation: major revision.** **Yes, MAJOR issues remain:** the central claim conflates local elasticity with the share of a belief–anchor gap, and the process-model conclusion is stronger than the model comparisons support. The reported sample-count arithmetic is consistent, and I found no clear numerical contradiction requiring a new analysis.
